title: Jon Scheyer explains why he turned down Mavericks, remains committed to Duke
content:
Jon Scheyer said he “wouldn’t be able to live with myself” if he left Duke without “seeing this through,” offering his most detailed public explanation yet for remaining with the Blue Devils after the Dallas Mavericks pursued him for their head-coaching vacancy this summer.

“I’m at a one-of-one place where not often you get your dream job when you’re 33,” Scheyer said Monday on the “Glue Guys” podcast. “And that’s what happened to me.”

Scheyer did not specifically name the Mavericks while discussing the NBA interest. Dallas, however, made multiple attempts to lure Scheyer away from Duke during its coaching search, ESPN reported in June. The Field of 68’s Jeff Goodman later reported that Scheyer had “major interest” in the Mavericks role but elected instead to return for a fifth season as Duke’s head coach.

The Mavericks ultimately hired Michigan coach Dusty May on June 22, just under three months after May led the Wolverines to their first national championship in 37 years.

Scheyer said his decision came down in part to a feeling that his work at Duke remains unfinished.

“I’m really proud of the start we’ve gone off to and the continuation of what has been built here,” he said. “But I think we’ve got so much left to do. We have so much left to accomplish.”

That feeling of unfinished business has been sharpened by two particularly painful NCAA Tournament exits in back-to-back years: Duke squandered a 14-point lead in the final eight minutes of its 2025 Final Four loss to eventual runners-up Houston, then blew a 19-point lead against UConn in last season’s Elite Eight before losing 73-72 on Braylon Mullins’ 35-footer with 0.4 seconds remaining.

Scheyer will get another chance this coming season with a Duke team that again expects to contend for a national championship.

Despite losing National Player of the Year Cameron Boozer to the NBA, the Blue Devils are returning several rotation pieces, and in the offseason they added Wisconsin transfer John Blackwell and signed the nation’s No. 2 recruiting class.

Scheyer, now 39, has gone 124-25 in four seasons since succeeding legendary coach Mike Krzyzewski in Durham. In addition to taking Duke to the Final Four in 2025 and the Elite Eight last season, he also played four seasons for the Blue Devils and helped them win the 2010 national championship before returning to the program as an assistant coach in 2013 and earning another title in 2015.

Durham, Scheyer said, has since become home.

“This is where my family is,” Scheyer said. “I’ve been in Durham longer than I grew up in Chicago at this point.”

Dallas’ interest in Scheyer also came with an obvious connection. Mavericks star Cooper Flagg, who is entering his second season after being crowned the league’s rookie of the year, spent his lone college season playing for Scheyer before Dallas selected him No. 1 in the 2025 NBA Draft. Former Duke center Dereck Lively II, who played for Scheyer in 2022-23, is also on the Mavericks’ roster.

Scheyer said considering an NBA opportunity ultimately strengthened his conviction about staying. Being “presented with something different,” he said, forced him to evaluate his situation at Duke and what the program still needed to improve.

“In some ways, it made me even stronger in terms of my dedication and what we have to do here,” Scheyer said. “I do think you want to double down on what you have to get right.”

He said the process “reenergized” and “refocused” him, including prompting him to examine Duke’s player-development philosophy and how the program builds its culture.

Scheyer stopped short of closing the door on an eventual move to the NBA. Acknowledging its status as the “highest level” of basketball, he made clear that, for now, he believes he is where he should be.

“In my own world,” Scheyer said, “I know this is where I’m supposed to be right now, doing what I’m doing with our guys. I love it.”
